doc.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995

chapter: Life on the road and advice
title: Thinking on your feet with unknown players
summary: On jazz parties and tours he must size up unfamiliar pianists and keep a large repertoire ready.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It’s interesting to go into these jazz parties and cruises and so forth that, like you said, you don’t have much control over who you’re going to play with. And the idea of having a repertory of tunes in your head I think is imposing to students who think about, well I know The Real Book or I know every sixth page of The Real Book or something. But you really have to have a pretty vast songlist in your head I would think, because you get into situations and —

You have to be able to think on your feet very quickly. I mean I’ll take a tour in England, I don’t know who I’m going to work with. And I could end up playing somewhere in the middle of the country with a pianist I’ve never seen before, who only knows — I’ve got to be able to look at this guy and figure what he’s going to know. And if I call a tune that he doesn’t know, I have to have another one immediately ready. Because I’m entertaining a roomful of people, I have to do this with a guy I’ve never met before. You have to find a way to keep everybody engaged, and this guy engaged. And sometimes it gets pretty tough. But you develop chops for it.
Right, chops, and your mental chops.

You walk on the stage prepared to think on your feet. And if that involves playing “Watermelon Man” all night long, that’s what you’re going to have to do. You may not be happy about it, but it’s got to be done.
